Sourdough starter, day by day

  • Day 0

    Mix 50g whole wheat flour with 50g warm water. Scrape down. Cover loosely.

  • Day 1

    Bubbles? Good. Do nothing but peek. A little hooch is normal.

    First feed: discard half, add 50g flour + 50g water. Stir well.

    Feed twice a day if it's bubbly. Look for a dome and a slightly tangy, yeasty smell.

Kettle Watch: the full boil, minute by minute

For user_name. One litre, lid on, no salt trickery.

  • 0:00

    Cold tap water in, lid down. Switch on. Nothing happens. Suspicious.

  • 0:45

    Faint hiss from the base. The element is warming and tiny bubbles cling to the walls.

  • 1:30

    A low roar builds and the bubbles detach. This is dissolved air escaping — not a boil yet.

  • 2:40

    Roar fades to a murmur, then near-silence. Confusing calm before the action.

  • 3:20

    Big rumble, bubbles streaming steadily, water gone slightly cloudy.

  • 3:50

    Rolling boil, 100 °C at sea level, lid dancing. Cut it now.

Why does it roar before it boils?

Dissolved air bubbles collapse as they rise, and that imploding roar is loudest at around 80 °C. Once that air is gone, the kettle quiets — the water still needs another few minutes.

Wooden flute: the honest first three weeks

For user_name, based on a typical C-pitch Irish flute.

  • Week 1

    You mostly make whistles and hiss. Goal: a clean note, any note. Embouchure is a tiny air-channel over the hole, not a puff.

  • Week 2

    Low D rings out on maybe one try in five. The flutters are an air-flow problem, not a talent problem.

  • Week 3

    Low G to A to B slide smoothly. You can find your embouchure from cold in under a minute.

A five-minute drill that actually works

Play one long note. Aim the airstream so the sound blooms — roll the flute out or in a hair. Do this for each of the six lowest notes once. Then stop. Better than an hour of noodling.

First tunes to try

Star of the County Down and The Foggy Dew sit nicely in the low octave and build breath control.

For user_name. Nine square metres of porcelain, one walk-in shower.

    Strip the old tiles, scrape adhesive, and vacuum. A cheap oscillating tool with a scraper blade earns its keep.

instances.html:
Blueberry bushes: what to do, and when

For user_name. Acid soil is the whole ballgame.

  • Late winter

    Prune hard: cut oldest stems to the base, thin crossing branches. You are building new fruiting wood.

  • Early spring

    Top up with pine bark mulch and a rhododendron feed. Never lime, never general garden compost near the roots.

  • Late spring

    Pollination overdrive. Two different varieties within a few metres doubles the crop.

  • Summer

    Water deeply twice a week if it is dry. Shallow roots hate drought, and so do the berries you are waiting for.

  • Autumn

    Leaves go red and orange, then drop. Pick up and bin fruit mummies to break pest cycles.

  • Again

    Expect the best harvest from the cuts you made two summers ago. Berries follow pruning with a lag.

Small berries? Three likely causes

Soil above pH 5.5, no pollinator variety nearby, or a dry June during the sizing stage. Fix in that order — it usually is the soil.

Sourdough pie crust: starter to slice

For user_name. One single-crust double batch.

  • Step 1

    Mix 250 g flour, 150 g cold butter cubes, 2 g salt, 100 g discard. Use a pie lifter to keep flat butter shards.

  • Step 2

    Bring together, then chill 30 minutes. Cold dough, hot oven. This is the rule you keep indiscretely true.

  • Step 3

    Roll and fold once or twice to build rough laminations. Chill again 20 minutes. Patience is the flake.

  • Step 4

    Roll to a round, line the tin, trim, and dock the base with a fork all over.

  • Step 5

    Blind-bake at 200 °C for 20 minutes with parchment and beans, then 8 minutes bare to dry the base.

  • Step 6

    Cool on a rack, fill and serve. The uncooked shell also freezes for a month.

What starter version should I use?

Any unfed discard works, but 100 % hydration is easiest to measure. It brings tang without the wait — the rest is all technique.

Rescue greyhound: the first week home

For user_name. Slow is fast with ex-racers.

  • Day 1

    Crate or quiet bed, daylight, minimal visitors. Offer water and a light meal. No baths, no big welcomes.

  • Day 2

    Leash walks only, on the same route. Count on a lot of standing and staring. That is progress, not failure.

  • Day 3

    Start a routine: out at 7am, meet, feed, nap. Greyhounds are creatures of pattern, like little striped statues.

  • Day 4

    Introduce stairs gently with a treat trail, one step at a time. Some take weeks. Stairs are the first real hurdle.

  • Day 5

    Begin short alone-time in another room, two minutes, then back. No long absences yet.

  • Day 7

    First settled nighttime. Most sleep through the night by now. If yours does not, slow down the day instead.

Near miss: calm might look like a happy dog who then explodes on a walk. Give 24–48 hours after new things. Greyhounds decompress quietly, then all at once.

A Year in the Hive

Northern-temperate apiary, roughly user_name's latitude. Every hive is its own small country with its own opinions.

  • Late winter

    Brood rearing restarts while snow is still on the ground. First cleansing flights on any day above 10 °C.

  • March

    Willow and hazel pollen. Feed thin syrup inside the hive or you'll wake the neighbours' hives too.

  • April

    Dandelion flow begins. First full inspection. Look for queen cells before they look for you.

  • May–June

    Main flow. Supers on. Checkerboard frames to give the queen room. Swarms possible any warm afternoon.

  • July

    Linden and bramble. Peak population, peak grumpiness.

  • August

    Harvest honey, leave 15 kg for winter. Treat for varroa once the supers are off.

  • September

    Ivory and heather top-ups. Feed thick syrup if stores are light.

  • October

    Cluster forms. Mouse guards on, entrances reduced, brood box closed until spring.

  • Winter

    Nothing. Resist the urge to open the lid. Heft the hive from behind instead.

Night One: What Actually Happens

Roughly. Yours will differ and that's normal. user_name, you will not sleep properly and it will still be fine.

  • 19:00

    You come home from the hospital. Baby falls asleep in the car seat. Every adult has a moment of "wait, are we allowed to just take it home?"

  • 20:00

    First feed attempt on your own sofa. Cluster feeding is common. Expect 8–12 feeds in 24 hours from here.

  • 21:30

    First solo nappy change. Have a spare nappy and spare onesie within arm's reach. Trust this one.

  • 22:00

    Baby is wide awake and inspecting the ceiling. Newborns don't know day from night yet. That comes around 6–8 weeks.

  • 01:00

    The fussy stretch. White noise, swaddle, dark room, on your chest upright after feeds if there's reflux.

  • 03:00

    Partner's shift. Whoever is awake does nappy + resettle; the other one sleeps properly, no half-sleeps.

  • 05:00

    Nappy count check: by day 5 you want at least 6 wet nappies a day. That's the only real dashboard.

  • 07:00

    First light, both of you still in yesterday's clothes. Congratulations, you've done night one.

  • Day 3–5

    Milk comes in for many people. Baby feeds and feeds and feeds. It gets easier.

Hot Sauce Ferment Log

3% brine by total weight (chilis + water). Using user_name's kitchen towel as the lid is optional but traditional.

  • Day 0

    Chilis, garlic, 3% salt by weight, enough water to keep everything under the brine. Weight it down.

  • Day 2

    First bubbles at the shoulder of the jar. That's the good fizz. No need to burp it if you used an airlock.

  • Day 5

    Sharp, raw smell eases into something rounder. Brine goes slightly cloudy. Normal. White film is kahm yeast — skim it, don't panic.

  • Day 8–10

    Taste it. It's the actual test. Fruity, tangy, still hot. If it's pleasant, keep going.

  • Day 14

    Active bubbling slows. pH should be 3.5 or lower — a cheap meter earns its keep here.

  • Day 18

    Blend the solids with some brine. Vinegar is optional now; the ferment already has acid.

  • Day 21

    Strain, bottle, fridge. It keeps for months and gets better for the first few weeks.

  • Any day

    Orange or pink fuzzy mould? Bin it. White film, pink or grey fuzz, no.

Callus Diary

The unglamorous part of learning guitar. Small print: thin strings hurt more than thick ones, so an acoustic is a character-building choice, user_name.

  • Day 1

    Fingertips go red and stingy after 15 minutes. Stop there. Sore is fine; bleeding is not.

  • Day 3

    A pale dent appears on each fingertip. This is the beginning. You are doing it right.

  • Week 1

    Fingers are tender but the initial bite has gone. Play 10-ish minutes twice a day; shorter is better than one long session.

  • Week 2

    Hard shiny patches. Barre chords are still unplayable and will be for a while. That's not a talent problem.

  • Week 3

    Real calluses. Chords ring cleanly for the first time without you watching each finger.

  • Week 4

    You overdid it and a callus peeled. Rough edge snagging the string? File it smooth, keep playing gently.

  • Week 6

    You stop noticing your fingers at all. That's the milestone. Your sound, however, still needs work — welcome to the long part.

Nights, Week by Week

A rule of thumb: puppies can hold their bladder roughly one hour per month of age, plus one. So a two-month-old gets about three hours max, user_name. Set an alarm before they do.

  • Night 1–3

    Crate or pen right next to your bed. They can smell you and it genuinely helps. Expect crying. Be boring and calm.

  • Night 4–7

    Take them out once or twice a night — quiet, no chat, straight back in. It is not playtime, however charming they are at 3am.

  • Week 2

    Whining settles faster. If it starts at a fixed time, that's your cue to pre-empt it by ten minutes.

  • Week 3–4

    Down to one night trip for many pups this age. Last water at about two hours before bed.

  • Week 6–8

    Six or seven solid hours becomes possible as they approach four months. Wait for them at the crate, don't let them bolt out.

  • Month 5–6

    Sleeping through, most nights. Any regression usually means a growth spurt, a new tooth, or a very exciting day.

  • Setback days

    Go back one step, don't shout it. Puppies remember tone far longer than they remember rules.

    Roots snaking out the drainage hole. Water runs straight through. A slight lean.

    Break up the root ball with your fingers. Don't be shy.

  • Replant

    Fresh soil, same depth. Press down. Water until it drains out the bottom.

    Keep it out of direct sun for a week. Expect a sulk. It'll bounce back.

Cold brew is just patience and a jar. Start tonight, drink tomorrow, user_name.

    Coarse grind. Roughly 1 part coffee to 4 parts water for concentrate, 1 to 8 for ready-to-drink.

Medium or dark roasts hold up. Light roasts can taste grassy over long steeps. Any cheap pre-ground is fine if it's coarse enough.

Keeping a Sourdough Starter Alive While You're Away

Starters are hardier than they look. Here's the minimum-effort plan, user_name.

  • Before you go

    Feed it one last time and let it sit out for an hour. Then it goes in the fridge.

  • Day 1-7

    Nothing. The cold slows everything down. A little liquid on top is normal, not a crisis.

  • Day 8-14

    If you're gone longer, take it out, pour off the dark liquid, feed, and put it back.

  • Return day

    Let it come to room temperature. Feed it and wait for bubbles before baking.

  • If it smells odd

    Pour off the top layer, feed with fresh flour and water. It usually comes back within two feeds.

Freezing as a backup

Spread a bit on parchment, freeze, and store the flakes in a bag. Thaw and feed to revive. It's not identical, but it's alive.

Neglect is not death. Starters survive weeks in the fridge. The worst that happens is a slower rise next time.

Scaffold boards are cheap, sturdy, and already look like shelves. Here's the order, user_name.

How many shelves to add

Three is a good default for paperback-sized gaps. Measure your tallest book and add a thumb's width.

Scaffold boards are usually 225mm wide. That's deep enough for most hardbacks, so you don't need to fuss over depth.

First week, no filter

The rules are simple: ten minutes, one jar, one bean. It gets loud around day four.

  • Day 1

    Soaked 200 g of dried chickpeas overnight. They swelled to nearly double. No bubbles yet, just wet legumes and hope.

  • Day 2

    Whizzed them with garlic, lemon, tahini, ice water. The ice water trick keeps it pale and fluffy. Still tastes like a good shop version.

  • Day 3

    Forgot the jar on the counter. Came home to a faint sour tang. That tang is the point, but it was too young to be pleasant.

  • Day 4

    First real bubbles. The smell turned from raw to bright. Ten minutes a day is doing its job.

  • Day 5

    Salt adjustment. Half a teaspoon more and the sourness snapped into focus. This is the batch you want to repeat.

  • Day 6

    Fed it a spoon of the liquid from the last jar. Yes, this is fermentation snobbery. Yes, it worked.

  • Day 7

    Tasted side by side with a supermarket tub. No contest. Yours has a finish; theirs has a shrug.

Why ice water and not tap?

Cold keeps the mixture from warming up and turning gluey while the blades run. If you must use tap, chill it in the fridge first. Same idea, slower.

A Month of Learning to Shuffle

Four weeks, fifteen minutes a day, no cards lost to the sofa. Probably.

  • Week 1

    Overhand shuffle only. Learn the grip: thumb on one corner, fingers on the other. Aim for a smooth bridge, not speed.

  • Week 2

    Riffle in the air, no release. Just bend and let them snap back. Ten minutes. Your wrists will complain.

    Half riffle, half overhand. Expect cards on the floor. Sweep, sigh, repeat.

  • Week 4

    Full riffle shuffle. Then bridge them together. The trick is a light touch, not strength.

What to do when cards stick

New decks are slick. Old decks clump. Wash your hands, and try a powder-free shuffle against a soft surface. It's not you, it's the cards.

    First full sentence. It'll be messy. You'll grin anyway.

Repeat any day you need. Morse rewards patience, not pride.

Two weeks, user_name, and the secret was less soap, more squeegee.

100% flour, 62% water, 2% salt, 0.5% instant yeast. Mix, rest 20 minutes, knead, then fridge for 2–3 days. Take out an hour before shaping.
